title: SLO-aware Degradation Orchestration and Customer-Impact Prioritization
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose:
This runbook defines an operational pattern we call 'SLO-aware degradation orchestration' — a coordinated, telemetry-driven process to gracefully degrade capabilities, prioritize customer impact, and preserve core SLOs during sustained load, partial failures, or capacity shortage events. The runbook prescribes decision criteria, tooling actions, and post-incident evidence required for each degradation step.

Audience:
- SRE on-call and escalation engineers
- Service owners and product leads for model-serving workloads
- Incident commanders and capacity planners

Scope:
Applies to multi-tenant inference services (hosted + dedicated pools) and routing/orchestration layers that can apply tiered degradation (e.g., caching-only, reduced model size, disabled non-essential features). Not intended for hardware-level triage or purely client-side issues.

Key goals:
- Keep customer-visible critical SLOs (P99 latency, availability) within target where feasible
- Minimize total user-impact (customers affected × severity) given limited capacity
- Provide clear, auditable actions and telemetry for post-incident review

Signals and SLOs to monitor (primary):
1) Availability SLO: request success rate (>= 99.95% 1h rolling)
2) Latency SLO: P95 <= 220ms, P99 <= 600ms (per model route)
3) Error budget consumption rate: burn rate > 3x on 30m window triggers action
4) Queue depth and worker saturation: queue_length > 1000 or GPU_util > 92%
5) KV cache hit rate: if hit_rate drops below 40% for 15m, prioritize cache warming

Decision matrix (summary)

Actions are grouped into Phases A → D. Each phase escalates customer-impact but reduces pressure on serving capacity. The on-call rota and incident commander must follow the numeric thresholds below.

Phase | Trigger (example) | Primary aim | Ownership
------|-------------------|------------|---------
A - Protect SLOs | Burn rate > 3x for 30m OR P99 crossing threshold | Tactical admission control, reclaim small headroom | SRE on-call
B - Reduce non-essential work | Sustained queue growth > 30m despite A | Disable best-effort routes / non-critical transforms | Service owner + SRE
C - Mixed-mode degradation | Multiple pools saturated, cross-region failover risk | Reroute to fallback models / reduce model size (quantized) | SRE + Runtime team
D - Customer-prioritized shutdown | Critical sustained violation and no capacity regain | Graceful throttle by customer priority and emergency credits | SRE, Customer Success

Detailed thresholds table (example values)

| Metric | Soft trigger | Hard trigger | Immediate action |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Error budget burn rate (30m) | > 2x | > 3x | Enter Phase A: apply token admission control (5%) |
| Cluster GPU util (5m avg) | 85% | 92% | Begin reclaiming idle models; warm fallback pools |
| P99 latency (route) | > 600ms | > 900ms | Step down to smaller model or enable fast-path cache |
| Queue length (per shard) | 500 | 1000 | Activate degraded routing and drop low-priority requests |

Operational playbook (step-by-step)

1) Initial detection (SRE on-call)
- Confirm signal: cross-check Prometheus graphs (p99, burn-rate, queue), recent deploys, and pod restart events.
- Triage scope: single region? single model route? tenant-scoped? Use the following query examples:
  - PromQL: sum(rate(request_errors[5m])) by (route) / sum(rate(request_total[5m])) by (route)
  - PromQL queue: max(queue_length) by (shard)

2) Enter Phase A — Protect SLOs (SRE on-call)
- Apply token-level admission control by setting admission policy to 'conservative' via /api/ops/admission (see CLI below).
- If using the traffic-shaper: reduce accepted concurrency for low-priority lanes by 20% and increase service-level timeouts to enable graceful backpressure.
- Communicate in incident channel: post short note with metrics and actions taken.

3) Evaluate and escalate to Phase B — Reduce non-essential work (service owner + SRE)
- Disable non-critical pipelines: e.g., turn off reranking, proactive streaming transforms, or offline evaluation hooks.
- Reclaim idle dedicated pools: drain long-idle VMs/GPUs and reallocate as burst capacity.
- Metrics to verify: drop in queue_length and burn-rate within 10–20 minutes.

4) Phase C — Mixed-mode (runtime intervention)
- Swap routes to small-model variants (e.g., model-v2-int8) using rollout policy 'degrade-fast'.
- If available, enable prefix KV cache prefill for heavy tenants.
- If cross-region, start controlled cross-region routing (max 10% traffic shift per 5 minutes).

5) Phase D — Customer prioritization and controlled shutdown
- Apply customer-priority gating: only top-tier tenants retain full routes. See Priority Buckets section below.
- Issue customer-facing communication templates (Customer Success owns outbound).
- Open emergency provisioning ticket for Dedicated expansion if contractual SLA impacted.

Customer Priority Buckets (example)
- P0: Enterprise with SLA > 99.9% - keep full access during Phase C, crediting on P99 breach
- P1: Large self-serve customers - reduced throughput but maintain best-effort latency
- P2: Free-tier and experimental buckets - accept higher degradation and bulk throttles

CLI and API examples

- Set admission policy (admin only):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPS_TOKEN" \
    -d '{"policy":"conservative","low_priority_reduction_pct":20}' \
    https://console.internal.redwood/api/ops/admission

- Swap model route to fallback variant:
  redwoodctl rollout set --route text-gen/standard --variant small-quantized --strategy degrade-fast

- Quick check of queue (kubectl):
  kubectl top pods -l app=inference-router -n inference | sort -k3 -nr | head -n 6

Telemetry and verification checklist (must complete after each phase change)
- Confirm P99 and burn-rate trends stabilized for 15 minutes
- Verify queue_length and GPU util decreased by at least 10% per step or document why not
- Record actions in incident timeline with timestamps and responsible engineer

Escalation criteria and owners
- If Phase A actions do not reduce burn rate within 20 minutes → escalates to SRE shift lead
- If Phase B actions do not recover capacity in 30 minutes → invite runtime and infra owners
- If Phase C fails and customer impact is significant → IC opens executive alert and Customer Success becomes primary comms owner

Post-incident evidence and postmortem requirements
- Required artifacts (submit to postmortem ticket within 48h):
  - Incident timeline with exact timestamps for each phase transition and admission control changes
  - Prometheus export (30m before to 2h after) for p50/p95/p99, burn-rate, queue_length, GPU metrics
  - Rollout logs for any model swaps and admission policy API calls
  - Customer impact matrix (tenants affected, duration, credits issued)

- RCA focus areas:
  - Why did automated signals not prevent escalation?
  - Were fallback model variants tested in the shadow environment?
  - Cost/latency tradeoffs and whether a different policy would have reduced customer-impact

Tooling integrations recommended
- Traffic-shaper: integrate with token-level metadata to support per-tenant throttles
- Admission control API: must be auditable and emit events to Incidents topic in Kafka
- Capacity dashboard: add a "degradation state" overlay that shows active phases per cluster

Runbook annex: Safe-mode quick commands
- Emergency permit for a single tenant to bypass throttles for 60 minutes:
  curl -X POST https://console.internal.redwood/api/ops/permits \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPS_TOKEN" -d '{"tenant":"acme-corp","ttl_minutes":60}'

- Rollback a degrade-fast rollout:
  redwoodctl rollout rollback --route text-gen/standard --to previous

Operational notes and best practices
- Test degradation paths during regular chaos windows: include model variant swaps and KV cache prefill flows in runbook rehearsals.
- Maintain a library of pre-approved customer messaging templates for each Priority Bucket.
- Prefer fast, observable steps early (admission control) before high-impact actions (customer shutdown).
- Keep experiment and canary traffic isolated from production tenant-critical lanes to avoid noisy neighbor failures.
